blocks.text: On the ravens that brought Elias bread and meat near the brook Cherith, 1 Reg. XVII, 3.

Now we must speak of Elias, to whom, while he was hiding at the brook Cherith near the Jordan, הערבים, the ravens, at God's command, brought bread and meat twice a day, 1 Reg. XVII, 3. 4. 5. 6. Because this has seemed scarcely credible to captious minds, there are those who deny that ravens are meant by the Hebrew word ערבים orebim. Thus, according to Kimchi, some explain it as merchants, as in Ezech. XXVII, 27., where we have ערבי מערבך, that is, those who trade in your wares. For others ערבים are Arabs, as in 2 Par. XXI, 16. and Nehem. IV, 1. In Bereshith Rabba, ch. 33, we read עיר היא בתחום ביתשאן ושמה ערבו, There is a town named Arabo in the vicinity of Bethshan (or Scythopolis), as Rabbi Judah writes; its citizens are thought to be called הערבים here. For the Arabic translator too, ערבים Orebim are not ravens but the name of a people. For he renders 1 Reg. XVII, 4.: I have commanded لعوربيم [li-ʿwrbym] the Orebimites to feed you. And in verse six: وكان العوربيم [wa-kāna al-ʿwrbym] And it came about that the Orebimites brought him bread and meat ^{(1)}. But it is easy to show that these interpretations have nothing sound in them. For although Ezekiel [II, 807] describes the Tyrian merchants with the periphrasis ערבי מערבך, those who trade in your wares, ערבים by itself nowhere means merchants. Nor would God have said in general terms, I have commanded merchants, but rather I have commanded the merchants of this or that place to feed you. The other renderings are refuted by the location of the place where this miracle occurred. For near the Jordan, where Elias was hiding, there were no Arabs, no Orebimites, nor any town named Arabo, as far as I know. Moreover, Arabs are not called ערבים Orebim in Hebrew, but ערבים Arbim; and as for the town ערבו Arabo, if there ever was one (which is not yet established to my satisfaction), its inhabitants would have been called ערבויים Arabojim ^{(2)}, not Orebim. Furthermore, Elias, ordered to hide there, would not truly have been hidden if the local inhabitants had known of his hiding place. And this hiding place would soon have been disclosed to King Ahab, who was searching for him everywhere with great care ^{(3)}.
